title: Latency-dollar trellis brief (sketch)
content:
Purpose and scope:

This is a working sketch for a short collateral piece (trellis-style) we can put in the Optimize collateral library: show tradeoffs between latency percentiles and incremental $/1k queries (or $/million tokens) for three common workload archetypes. The goal is a simple visual/text artifact product/content/solutions can use when talking to customers about SLA tiering and cost knobs.

Notes on data provenance (quick):
- Microbench harness run on internal stage cluster (n4-gpu-equivalent).
- Model: open-llm-v2-13b quantized Q4_0 baseline and Q4_1 variant used for low-cost lane.
- Request mix: 30% short (<=16 tokens), 50% medium (32–128), 20% long (256–512).
- Two serving configs: small-batch (batch size 1–4, low tail) and packed-mode (batch size up to 64, high throughput).
- Costs estimated from current Dedicated reserved capacity pricing + amortized infra overhead. These are draft numbers for internal comparison only.

Archetypes and scenarios (what to compare):
A) Conversational microinteractions (latency-sensitive): tight p95/p99 goals; most QPS is short-medium tokens.
B) Document-summarization (throughput favored): longer tokens; tolerant of higher p99 but want low average $/Q.
C) Hybrid chat-batch (mixed; need p50 low, p95 moderate).

Trellis layout (how to read):
- Each small cell is a scenario slice (A/B/C) x serving mode (small-batch / packed-mode) x quant profile (baseline / low-cost).
- X-axis: incremental $ per 1k queries (left = cheaper).
- Y-axis: latency percentile (ms). We show three percentiles as lines: P50, P95, P99.

ASCII trellis (compact representation) — numbers are illustrative (rounded):

Legend: $/1k = dollars per 1000 queries; latency in ms.

Scenario A - conversational (short-medium mix)
Mode: small-batch (low tail)
Costs: baseline $/1k=0.95 | low-cost $/1k=0.62

   $/1k -> 0.6     0.8     1.0
P50    |   50 ms  46 ms  42 ms
P95    |  120 ms 100 ms  90 ms
P99    |  210 ms 170 ms 150 ms

Interpretation: low-cost quantization reduces cost by ~35% but increases p99 by ~25–30% in small-batch mode for short interactions. P50 improves slightly due to lower kernel overhead on some kernels.

Scenario A - conversational
Mode: packed-mode (high throughput)
Costs: baseline $/1k=0.38 | low-cost $/1k=0.26

   $/1k -> 0.26    0.32    0.38
P50    |   55 ms  51 ms  48 ms
P95    |  260 ms 210 ms 180 ms
P99    |  860 ms 650 ms 420 ms

Interpretation: packed-mode gives big $ savings per 1k but amplifies tail for conversational workloads. If customers have strict p99 SLOs, packed-mode needs supplemental fallbacks or admission control.

Scenario B - doc summarization (long requests)
Mode: small-batch
Costs: baseline $/1k=3.40 | low-cost $/1k=2.10

   $/1k -> 2.1    2.7    3.4
P50    |  840 ms  760 ms  700 ms
P95    | 1300 ms 1200 ms 1100 ms
P99    | 2200 ms 2000 ms 1800 ms

Interpretation: long-request workloads are dominated by decode time; quant helps cost significantly with modest latency degradation but p99 stays high across modes. For throughput purchases, packed-mode yields better $ but needs pipeline-level batching safeguards.

Scenario C - hybrid chat-batch (mixed lengths)
Mode: packed-mode
Costs: baseline $/1k=1.20 | low-cost $/1k=0.78

   $/1k -> 0.78   1.0    1.2
P50    |  180 ms 160 ms 145 ms
P95    | 540 ms 450 ms 380 ms
P99    |1200 ms 980 ms 700 ms

Interpretation: mixed workloads show non-linear tail amplification under packed-mode; p99 swing is large moving toward cheaper configs.

Short textual charts (sparklines) to use in slides or product pages:
- "Conversational small-batch": P50 ▂▃▅▆ | P95 ▂▄▆▇ | P99 ▂▁▂▃ (cost up -> latency down)
- "Packed throughput": P50 ▃▅▆▆ | P95 ▂▂▃▅ | P99 ▁▁▂▇ (cheaper -> much worse tail)

Key takeaways (for collateral):
- Cost-per-query and tail latency trade are workload-dependent. Short token interactions are most sensitive to packed-mode tail amplification.
- Quantization/low-cost kernels give clear $ wins but can hurt p99 in high-concurrency packing; need to pair with admission/fallback rules.
- Small-batch mode is the predictable path for conversational SLOs (higher $/1k but much tighter p99).
- For bulk/throughput tasks (long documents), prioritize packing and queuing; optimize decode pipelines instead of prioritizing single-request p99.

Recommended messaging snippets (short):
- "Pick the lane: small-batch for SLA-critical chat, packed-mode for throughput-bound jobs — we give you knobs to tune both."
- "Quant profiles reduce unit cost by 25–40% in our tests; pairing them with SLO-aware routing recovers most tail risk."

Open questions / experiments to run next (tracking JIRA-OPT-4123):
- Measure tail under heterogeneous GPU families (A100 vs L4-equivalent). Current run is single-hardware.
- Try hybrid decode prefetching (predictive KV cache priming) for conversational packed-mode to see if p99 gap shrinks.
- End-to-end cost model that includes network ingress/egress for private deployments.

Design notes for final collateral:
- Create 3x2 trellis image: rows = Archetypes (A/B/C), cols = Mode (small-batch, packed). Put dollar axis at bottom and show P50/P95/P99 lines with shaded uncertainty band.
- Add short callout per cell with quick recommendation (1 sentence).
- Keep the one-pager to a single A4/letter; augment with a longer appendix that contains full numeric tables and test harness config.

Quick action items:

- Leah: draft product copy variants for web and sales one-pager (due 2029-05-24).

-- end of sketch --
